## Regression

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(tmap)
library(corrplot)  
library(car)      
library(lmtest)    
library(sjPlot)    
library(spdep)    
```

**Overview:**
This lab focuses on regression techniques. You'll be analyzing the association of various land cover, vegetation, climate, and terrain characteristics with summer land surface temperature (LST) in tracts across California, Oregon, and Washington. The goal is to understand which characteristics of places are associated with urban heat, and how well a linear regression model can explain it.

### Data and research questions

Let's import the dataset.

```{r}
lab6_data<-st_read("data/lab6_gee_lstdata.gpkg")
```

The variables in the dataset are:

* GISJOIN: Unique tract identifier from NHGIS (2024)
* lst_c: Land surface temperature (C), the median of clear-sky Landsat 8/9 observations from June-August 2021. This is the thermal "skin" temperature of the surface at the satellite overpass (late morning), not air temperature.
* ndvi: Normalized difference vegetation index from Landsat (June-August 2021 median). Values range from -1 to 1, with higher values indicating more vegetation.
* ndbi: Normalized difference built-up index from Landsat (June-August 2021 median). Higher values indicate more built-up or bare surfaces.
* ndwi: Normalized difference water index from Landsat (June-August 2021 median). Higher values indicate more water or moisture.
* impervious_pct: Percent of the 30 m pixel covered by impervious surface (data from the 2021 National Land Cover Database)
* tree_cover_pct: Percent tree canopy cover (data from MODIS Vegetation Continuous Fields, 250 m resolution)
* prism_tmean_c: Mean air temperature (C) from June-August 2021 (data from PRISM, 4 km resolution)
* prism_ppt_mm: Total precipitation (mm) from June-August 2021 (data from PRISM, 4 km resolution)
* elevation: Elevation in meters (data from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission/NASA)
* slope: Terrain slope in degrees, derived from the elevation data
* nlcd_class/nlcd_label: Land cover class code and label (data from the 2021 National Land Cover Database)
* developed: 1 if the land cover class at the centroid is one of the NLCD developed classes (21-24), 0 otherwise

Our primary research question is how the vegetation, land cover, climate, and terrain variables in our dataset are predictive of land surface temperature. Note that the variables come from different sources at different spatial resolutions, and that the sample is dominated by developed areas (a large majority of tracts are in developed land cover classes), so our results speak most directly to urban and suburban heat.

```{r rescale}
lab6_data <- lab6_data %>%
  mutate(ndvi_10  = ndvi * 10,            # per 0.1 of NDVI
         imperv10 = impervious_pct / 10,  # per 10 percentage points
         tree10   = tree_cover_pct / 10,  # per 10 percentage points
         ppt10    = prism_ppt_mm / 10,    # per 10 mm of rain
         elev100  = elevation / 100)      # per 100 m
```

### Part 1: Analysis of summer 2021 data

We will start by exploring the distribution of our variables.

**Question 1** _Create histograms for LST, NDVI, impervious surface, tree cover, precipitation, slope, and elevation. Based on these graphs, assess the normality of these variables._

```{r}
# Reset graphics
graphics.off()

# Histograms
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))

hist(lab6_data$lst_c,
     main = "LST",
     xlab = "LST (degrees C)",
     col = "tomato",
     border = "white")

hist(lab6_data$ndvi,
     main = "NDVI",
     xlab = "NDVI",
     col = "forestgreen",
     border = "white")

hist(lab6_data$impervious_pct,
     main = "Impervious Surface",
     xlab = "Percent",
     col = "goldenrod",
     border = "white")

hist(lab6_data$tree_cover_pct,
     main = "Tree Cover",
     xlab = "Percent",
     col = "mediumseagreen",
     border = "white")

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))

hist(lab6_data$prism_ppt_mm,
     main = "Summer Precipitation",
     xlab = "Millimeters",
     col = "dodgerblue",
     border = "white")

hist(lab6_data$slope,
     main = "Slope",
     xlab = "Degrees",
     col = "mediumpurple",
     border = "white")

hist(lab6_data$elevation,
     main = "Elevation",
     xlab = "Meters",
     col = "darkorange",
     border = "white")

# Reset plotting layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

{Based on the histograms, LST is approximately normally distributed, with a bell-shaped curve and most values around 40 to 50°C. NDVI is slightly right-skewed, with most values between 0.2 and 0.4. Impervious surface is not normally distributed: its values cluster near 0% and again at 50 to 70%. Tree cover, precipitation, slope, and elevation are all strongly right-skewed. Most observations have low values, and only a few have very high ones.}

**Question 3** _Based on the maps from question 2, summarise major patterns you see in the spatial distribution of these data from any of your variables of interest. How do they appear to be associated with the LST variable?_

{From the maps, I observed that LST follows a clear regional pattern across the study area. Temperatures generally decrease from south to north and from inland areas toward the coast. The highest LST values (49.74–65.83 C) are mainly concentrated in the southern and southeastern regions, while the lowest values (10.54–31.67 C) are mostly found along the coast and in the northwestern regions.NDVI, tree cover, and precipitation show similar spatial patterns that are almost opposite to the LST pattern. Northern and western regions have more vegetation, higher tree cover, and greater precipitation, while southern and southeastern regions are generally drier, less vegetated, and hotter. This suggests a negative relationship between these variables and LST. Interestingly, impervious surfaces do not follow the same regional pattern. Higher percentages of impervious surfaces appear scattered across urban areas rather than being concentrated in the hottest regions. Some areas with low percentages of impervious surfaces still experience high LST. Therefore, the relationship between impervious surfaces and LST is not very clear from the maps. Slope and elevation mainly reflect the distribution of mountainous regions. Areas with steeper slopes generally appear to have lower LST. However, elevation shows a mixed pattern, as some inland areas with higher elevations also experience relatively high temperatures. Based on my observations, I would expect NDVI, tree cover, and precipitation to have strong negative relationships with LST, slope to have a possible negative relationship, and impervious surfaces to have a weak relationship. The relationship between elevation and LST remains unclear. However, further statistical analysis would be needed to confirm these observations.}

**Question 4** _Create univariate models for each of the variables listed in question 1, with LST as the dependent variable. Print the summary of each model. Write a summary of those results that indicates the direction, magnitude, and significance for each model coefficient._

```{r}
model_ndvi <- lm(lst_c ~ ndvi, data = lab6_data)
model_impervious <- lm(lst_c ~ impervious_pct, data = lab6_data)
model_tree <- lm(lst_c ~ tree_cover_pct, data = lab6_data)
model_ppt <- lm(lst_c ~ prism_ppt_mm, data = lab6_data)
model_slope <- lm(lst_c ~ slope, data = lab6_data)
model_elevation <- lm(lst_c ~ elevation, data = lab6_data)

summary(model_ndvi)
summary(model_impervious)
summary(model_tree)
summary(model_ppt)
summary(model_slope)
summary(model_elevation)
```

{From the regression results, I observed that all six variables have statistically significant relationships with LST since their p-values are less than 0.05. However, some variables explain the variation in LST better than others. Tree cover has the strongest relationship with LST, explaining about 58.69% of its variation, followed by NDVI, which explains 47.76%. Both variables have negative coefficients, meaning that areas with more vegetation and tree cover tend to have lower surface temperatures. This agrees with what I observed in the maps in Question 3. Precipitation and slope also have negative relationships with LST, explaining 29.52% and 13.06% of its variation, respectively. This suggests that wetter areas and areas with steeper slopes tend to have lower surface temperatures. Impervious surface has a positive relationship with LST, which is expected because surfaces such as roads and buildings absorb and retain heat. However, it only explains 4.85% of the variation in LST, indicating a weak relationship. I found the elevation result interesting because I expected LST to decrease as elevation increased. Instead, the results show a weak positive relationship, explaining only 1.78% of the variation in LST. Tree cover and NDVI are the best individual predictors of LST, while impervious surface and elevation are the weakest. Most of these results agree with my observations from the maps. However, since the variables were analyzed separately, it would be interesting to see how their relationships with LST change when they are included together in a multiple linear regression model.}

**Question 5** _Create a multivariate regression model with the variables of interest, choosing EITHER NDVI or tree cover (but not both), since both measure vegetation. You may also choose to leave out any variables that were insignificant in Q4. Use the univariate models as your guide. Print the summary of the model._

```{r}
model_all <- lm(lst_c ~ ndvi + impervious_pct + prism_ppt_mm +
                  slope + elevation, data = lab6_data)
summary(model_all)
```

**Question 6** _Summarize the results of the multivariate model. What are the direction, magnitude, and significance of each coefficient? How did it change from the univariate models you created in Q4 (if at all)? What do the R2 and F-statistic values tell you about overall model fit?_

{I included NDVI, impervious surface, precipitation, slope, and elevation in the multivariate model. I excluded tree cover because it is strongly correlated with NDVI (r = 0.83). All five variables are statistically significant (p < 0.001). NDVI has a negative coefficient of -24.85, meaning that a 0.1-unit increase in NDVI is associated with a 2.49 C decrease in LST. Precipitation and slope also have negative coefficients of -0.0356 and -0.4219, respectively. Elevation has a positive coefficient of 0.0042, meaning that a 100 m increase in elevation is associated with a 0.42 C increase in LST, while holding the other variables constant. Compared to Question 4, the NDVI coefficient changed slightly, while the negative coefficients of precipitation and slope became smaller in magnitude. The positive coefficient of elevation increased slightly. Interestingly, impervious surface changed from a positive coefficient of 0.0535 to a negative coefficient of -0.0632. This may be due to its relationship with other environmental variables and regional differences. It does not necessarily mean that impervious surfaces reduce LST. The R-squared value of 0.6099 and adjusted R-squared value of 0.6098 show that the model explains approximately 61% of the variation in LST, leaving 39% unexplained. The F-statistic of 3700, with a p-value less than 0.001, indicates that the overall model is statistically significant and fits the data better than a model without predictors.}

**Question 7** _Use a histogram and a map to assess the normality of residuals and any spatial autocorrelation. Summarise any notable patterns that you see._

```{r q7, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.width=9}

# Calculate residuals from the multivariate model
lab6_data$residuals <- lab6_data$lst_c - predict(model_all, newdata = lab6_data)

# Histogram of residuals
hist(lab6_data$residuals,
     main = "Histogram of Residuals",
     xlab = "Residuals (C)",
     ylab = "Frequency",
     col = "steelblue",
     border = "white",
     breaks = 40)

# Add a reference line at zero
abline(v = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

# Summary of residuals
summary(lab6_data$residuals)

# Map of residuals
tmap_mode("plot")

map_residuals <- tm_shape(lab6_data) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "residuals",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "fixed",
      breaks = c(-30, -10, -5, -2, 2, 5, 10, 30),
      values = "-brewer.rd_bu",
      midpoint = NA
    ),
    col_alpha = 0,
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Residuals (C)",
      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")
    )
  ) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

map_residuals

```

{From the histogram, I observed that the residuals form a bell shape centered on zero, with a mean of 0.00 C and a median of 0.11 C. Most values sit close to zero. The shape is not quite normal, though, because the negative tail runs longer than the positive one. Residuals range from -26.62C to 17.62C, so the model's largest errors are overpredictions. The residual map shows that the residuals are not randomly distributed. Positive residuals (red) cluster in southern California, where the model tends to underestimate LST. Negative residuals (blue) are more common in central and parts of northern California, where it tends to overestimate. Clusters of similar residual values indicate positive spatial autocorrelation, meaning neighboring census tracts have similar prediction errors. That pattern also suggests the model does not capture some regional factors affecting LST. The normality assumption is reasonably satisfied, but the spatial independence assumption is not.}

**Question 8** _Assess any issues with multicollinearity or heteroskedastity in this model using the techniques shown in class. Run the appropriate tests and explain what their results show you._

```{r}
vif(model_all)

cor(lab6_data %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      select(ndvi, impervious_pct, prism_ppt_mm, slope, elevation))

bptest(model_all)

plot(model_all, which = 1)
```

{From the VIF results, I noticed that all the values are below 5, ranging from 1.32 to 2.72. This suggests that multicollinearity is not a major issue in the model. The correlation matrix also shows that NDVI is positively correlated with precipitation (0.63) and negatively correlated with impervious surface (-0.60). Although some of the variables are related, their correlations are not strong enough to suggest a serious multicollinearity problem. The Breusch-Pagan test gave a statistic of 244.91 and a p-value less than 0.001. Since the p-value is below 0.05, I reject the null hypothesis and conclude that heteroskedasticity is present in the model.Looking at the residuals versus fitted values plot, I noticed that the residuals are not evenly spread around zero. The spread becomes wider between 40°C and 50°C, and there are also a few extreme negative residuals. This supports the results of the Breusch-Pagan test. I would conclude that multicollinearity is not a major concern, but heteroskedasticity is a problem in the model because the variance of the residuals is not constant. This may affect the accuracy of the standard errors and significance tests.}

**Question 9** _How would you summarise the results of this model in a sentence or two? In addition, looking at the full model and your diagnostics, do you feel this is a model that provides meaningful results? Explain your answer. As part of your answer, consider that NDVI (or tree cover), impervious surface, and LST are all derived from satellite data, and that neighboring tracts tend to have similar values. How might each of these affect how you interpret the model?_

{Across 11,837 census tracts, higher NDVI, summer precipitation, and slope are associated with lower LST, while elevation is associated with higher LST after adjusting for the other variables; the five-predictor model explains about 61% of LST variation. Impervious surface has a surprising negative adjusted coefficient even though its simple relationship with LST is positive. I think the model provides a useful descriptive starting point, but it should not be treated as evidence of cause and effect or a fully reliable predictive model. NDVI, impervious cover, and LST are all derived partly from satellite observations and may share spatial patterns, measurement limitations, and differences in resolution. Also, neighboring tracts can be more similar than distant tracts, so the residuals may not be independent. The residual map suggests this spatial clustering, and the Breusch-Pagan test indicates nonconstant error variance. These issues mean the conventional p-values can be overly optimistic. Regional climate and other omitted factors could also explain the sign reversal for impervious surface. I would therefore use the model to describe associations, not to claim that changing one land-cover variable would directly produce the estimated LST change.}
